title: States of Matter

1.title: Experiment 1: does it keep its shape?

q.Table: 1 (a, b). Did each one keep its own shape in both containers?
q.1 (c): 1 (c). The water looked different in the two containers. Was there still the same AMOUNT of water? Explain how you know.

q.2 (a): 2 (a). Copy the table (What is inside · Volume at the start · Volume after pushing · Did it squash?) and record your results.
q.2 (c): 2 (c). You pushed just as hard on both. Why is that important?

q.3 (a): 3 (a). Nobody stirred the water. Describe what happened to the drop of colour after 3 minutes.
q.3 (b): 3 (b). How long did it take before you could smell the perfume? How far is your desk from the front, in big steps?
q.3 (c): 3 (c). Nobody carried the smell to your desk. So how did it get there?

q.4 (a): 4 (a). Explain why the water took the shape of the container but the stone did not. Use the word particles.
q.4 (b): 4 (b). Explain why the air squashed but the water did not. Use the words gaps and particles.
q.Table: 4 (c). Which state of matter carried the perfume smell across the room?

q.5 (a): 5 (a). Give one thing a SOLID does that a liquid does not.
q.5 (b): 5 (b). Give one thing a GAS does that a liquid does not.
q.Table: Sort. Which state is each one at room temperature?
q.5 (c): 5 (c). Which experiment did you find the most surprising, and why?

q.Reflect: Reflect. Explain to a younger child, in two sentences, why you can squash air but not water.
q.Revision plan: Anything not ticked is your revision list. Which will you revise first, and how?
